answer:
English is nearly impossible to avoid in everyday life. We hear it on television and in song lyrics, study it at school, and for many people, use it at work. This constant exposure gives us a fairly good sense of how the language works. I think most people understand at least some English, and quite a few are probably very proficient. However, when I consider my own abilities, it is clear that I am more confident in the passive skills of reading and listening than in writing and speaking.

Throughout my education, from elementary school through upper secondary school, my teachers have always emphasized writing. In upper secondary school especially, we wrote many essays and reviews. Yet despite all that practice, I still struggle with writing in English. Spelling can be difficult, of course, but the bigger problem, in my view, is grammar. Grammatical errors are often complicated and harder to resolve than spelling questions, which can usually be answered by looking up a word in a dictionary.

We did not get much practice in reading at school. We had textbooks, of course, but their articles were often very short and covered unrelated topics, giving the impression that they had been taken out of context. In other words, the textbooks were boring. We also read several works of literature and wrote reviews of them. I think reading literature is a tremendously rewarding way to become more fluent in a language. It also helped me when I studied religious studies, since much of the course material was in English.

My greatest difficulty with reading arises when I encounter texts written in specialized language. Reading an English text that would be challenging even in Swedish is a real test, and it can take a great deal of time. This brings me to another problem: my patience, or rather, my lack of it. Naturally, reading in English is slower than reading in Swedish, at least at first, but for some reason I find that hard to accept.

Speaking and listening are obviously closely related. Still, I think listening is the easiest of the four skills, while speaking is the most difficult. This is undoubtedly because we get much more practice listening, especially through television and music, than we do speaking. We do not understand every word, of course, but we can usually follow the general meaning. Even so, specialized language can be just as challenging to understand when spoken as it is in writing.

As I mentioned above, my biggest difficulty with English is speaking. I have had little real experience speaking English because I have never spent an extended period abroad. Nor did I get much speaking practice at school, where English lessons were based primarily, if not exclusively, on theory. If anything, school made me even more reluctant to speak. You become so preoccupied with getting every grammatical detail right that you are afraid to open your mouth for fear of being laughed at. I know this sounds discouraging, and it probably does not apply to everyone. On the other hand, I believe those fears would disappear quite quickly if you simply started speaking.

Having completed this assignment, I have to say that it is difficult to assess my own abilities in the four language skills. I have never had trouble earning good grades in English at school, but I firmly believe that grades rarely reflect what someone actually knows. All I know is that language involves many different skills, and I would like to improve in all of them.
